Orrin Keepnews

Orrin Keepnews was born in New York City on March 2, 1923. He has played an important role in jazz as a record producer, writer and as a creative force with Riverside, Milestone and Landmark Records. Orrin produced classic recordings with Thelonious Monk, Bill Evans and Cannonball Adderley and continues to work in jazz from his home in San Francisco.
Orrin was interviewed in San Francisco, California on August 7, 2002 by Monk Rowe, Director of the Hamilton College Jazz Archive.

My name is Monk Rowe and we are in San Francisco filming for the Hamilton College Jazz Archive. I’m extremely pleased to be speaking with Orrin Keepnews today and trying to figure out how to introduce you, you’re a lot of things, writer, producer and —

I tend to think of myself primarily at least as a producer, and that’s the way I would prefer to be remembered. If I were to have a gravestone that’s what it should — if it gives occupation on gravestones, that’s what I want.
Right. Well I have to congratulate you on the contribution you’ve made to the art form called jazz. It’s really quite amazing the things you’ve been involved in and the careers that you have helped.

Well I must admit that I look back on it with a good deal of satisfaction. I’ve been very fortunate because in this business in particular, a lot of the associations that you form, at least initially, are accidental as hell. If someone tells me that I have been helpful to this or that career that’s exactly the thing that I want to hear because I have always looked on the role of the producer in a very specific way. Now one of the hardest things, and I’ve been at it, I’m getting perilously close to my fiftieth anniversary in this business, but I still have to pause usually when I’m asked to make some kind of definition of what it is I do, because for better or worse, I don’t know about other things because I’ve only done this really, but jazz record producers do a little bit of everything, as there is always a shortage of personnel, and it’s to me, the most important role is what I have taken to repetitiously referring to as being a catalytic agent. That I am supposed to create the circumstances under which the artist can work most effectively. That is, I’ve finally got it boiled down to that one mantra and that’s what I am, that’s what I do. I think one of the great things about — that statement is generally true, but the details of its implementation are constantly changing. There are no — almost literally — there are no two artists who can be dealt with in the same way. There are perhaps no two record dates that can be dealt with in the same way. That may be pushing it a little bit, but fundamentally that to me is what the continuing challenge is all about, that’s why I didn’t get bored a long time ago © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

with doing this. The only real serious variation is that I have — I used to say in recent years — but for a lot of years, a lot of my attention has been focused on reissues and obviously the procedures are a little different there. For the most part that makes it possible to get into cliches like well I spent the whole day in the studio with Louis Armstrong or Duke Ellington or Fats Waller, and he didn’t give me a hard time. But that joke got busted about a year ago because one of my most recent reissue projects was with Artie Shaw, who is now 92, is quite firmly there, could not possibly have ever been more opinionated in his life than he is now, and so I could not say I spent the day with Artie Shaw and he did not give me a hard time. He did give me a hard time. But it was a wonderful experience working with him actually, and it literally I think it’s about the only circumstances under which you can be working on pre-tape material with the artist. And there ain’t too many people who still have firm opinions, he still doesn’t like “Begin the Beguine,” which after all I guess was a 1937 or 8 recording. Maybe it was ’36. I don’t have to remember those things, they’re all firmly written down. Those discographies are unchanging. But what I consider the most important work has been the things that I’ve been able to do with a very large handful of artists who are important, whose work is and should be lasting and you know I know for a minute that it’s not my creativity. My job was to do two things. One is to appreciate and the other is to facilitate. And I usually don’t use such glorious words to describe it but I’ve always been the guy that was able to get it done, which kind of surprises me sometimes. I don’t think of myself as being firm, as being decision-maker, I certainly do not believe in the auteur theory of jazz direction, I don’t think, and there have been people and we won’t bother to name names but there have been other jazz record producers who clearly do think of themselves as king makers. And I never did. It just got to be the point of hey, somebody’s got to make the decision and okay, that’s one of the things that I’m here for. Sometimes you might make decisions because nobody else is even in the position to even be aware of the need for a decision. Initially I learned I guess — well let me say this — everything I learned initially I learned from the best possible teacher as far as I’m concerned. I owe my entire career, whatever success I may have, the man that is firmly responsible for that is Thelonious Monk. There is no question in my mind that I gained tremendously from the initially very frightening fact that this was the first artist of any significance who I worked with. I mean I had done a few things — before I got involved with Thelonious I had been in the studio with people like Randy Weston, Mundell Lowe, Billy Taylor, you know all pussycats. But here was a real tough cookie. Here was a man who knew what he wanted, thought he knew exactly how to get it, frequently was right, and the example I used to use, in other words the old fashion way of teaching a child to swim is you toss him into the deep end of the pool and if he doesn’t go under he’s learned to swim. Well I learned — that’s © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

exactly how I learned to swim. And it was, I also will say that, I said it many years ago with what I have learned I would never entrust as valuable and volatile a commodity as Thelonious to anybody as totally ignorant and inexperienced as I was at the time. But fortunately one of the great advantages of that, well basically it’s a 1950s phenomenon primarily, it happened a little before that, it happened a little after that, but the idea of the jazz fan as self-made jazz record producer actually the art owes a great deal to that phenomenon and a number of very important — Alfred Lion comes to mind, Milt Gabler, Lester Koenig at Contemporary Records. I don’t want to start naming names because you always leave out what you shouldn’t. But practically everybody, and it was very frequently exactly the same circumstances. If it was your company and you said you were the producer, there wasn’t anybody that was going to tell you you weren’t. So you did it. And most of us I must admit were self-appointed. Because I had a partner and Bill Grauer was initially a man, he was a serious jazz record collector and knew a hell of a lot more than I did about things but he naturally gravitated toward the business end of the company and so suddenly I found myself the creative director of Riverside Records and I made the most of it. The Monk experience taught me, quite seriously, not only how to behave in the presence of genius of a major artist, how to work effectively or hopefully effectively with somebody like that, and how to accomplish what you feel you have to accomplish in the face of who and what that artist is. And having survived Monk I have been fond of saying I could never again be frightened of any jazz musician. So it was, quite seriously, Sonny Rollins once in an interview with somebody, I think Stanley Crouch interviewed him at one point and Sonny, who of course during one of his sabbatical periods had spent some time in India, said that he thought that Monk was not a teacher so much as he was a guru, in the sense that a guru is somebody who enables you to bring out the best qualities in yourself. And Mr. Rollins, who is in addition to being an extremely articulate player, is also an extremely articulate thinker and expresser in words, this was a very specific point that Sonny was making and I think it’s incredibly accurate. Of course Monk has never had a student per se and never had. One of the true marks of an important person is that you will continue indefinitely to refer to them in the present tense. And I think that’s not just a slip. It may initially be that, but there are a lot of people — one of the glories of — thank God they invented the phonograph record. It keeps people very much alive. And unfortunately they haven’t worked out a way where they can vary what’s on the records, but in a sense we have with all of the emphasis on alternate takes that’s come about and the reissue scene. But these people are, the ones who remain a living presence, I still have that same attitude that combination of respect and veneration and pride, I do feel proud of what I have been able to help them to accomplish. I know damn well that there are circumstances, I don’t have to be immodest © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

about it, in which if not for me and the record company that I was operating and the way in which we proceeded with things — certainly a lot of careers would not have happened in the same way. I’m not saying that it wouldn’t have happened, but knowing what I do about — I’ll tell you, knowing what I do about some of the personalities that I dealt with I still haven’t figured out whether it was just luck of the draw or whether this is a more prevalent attitude than anybody appreciates but I sure have had a run of artists who never really believed that they have played it right. Who have to do another take because they didn’t get it yet, they haven’t done the best that they can do. And it’s amazing, I mean it’s a perfectly good description of Rollins, of Wes Montgomery, of Bill Evans. That’s a pretty good round up there. We used to have a standing joke about the creation, for recording purposes of a demon band, which would be made up of all of these people who never believed that they had done anything properly. There were a number of other people who I didn’t necessarily work much with directly but who were in the same category, J.J. Johnson, Percy Heath, a lot of people. And we were going to form this dream band as it were, there were two problems. One is obviously with that band you would never get an acceptable take on even one tune, and secondly you wouldn’t be able to find a drummer for that band. Drummers do not suffer from this problem. But other than that, that’s one of the major characteristics of jazz in my time anyhow. Well among other things, I mean somebody’s got to say hey, enough of this, let’s quit crapping around and go on to the next tune. Or, take my word for it, I really think we’ve got it there. One or the other of those takes has got it and we can always edit, but believe me let’s go on. And frequently the musician has no choice but to believe you, and so—
Let me ask you, what was in your childhood that steered you into jazz listening as a hobby first?
I don’t have the faintest idea.
Really.

I come from a totally non-musical family background. I remember quite distinctly that when I was about six a relative was breaking up a household and had a piano that she was willing to give to us and my mother said if we have a piano in the house, will you take lessons, which was a pretty stupid question for my mother to ask me, and I said hell no, or whatever a 6-year-old said, the equivalent of that, to my mother. And so I grew up quite non-musical. But what you have to remember is that when I was growing up there we were in the 30s. One of the advantages of being my age, there was an awful lot of remarkably good music on the radio. There were some pretty wonderful — the big band situation. In my recent experience with Artie Shaw I was able to point out to him, I was barely a teenager when he was first becoming a star. I said in my day if you were at all interested in music you could not equivocate. For example, you had to either be for © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

Benny Goodman or for Artie Shaw. You couldn’t waffle on that. And Artie, among other things has a wonderful sense of humor but not about himself. His response to that was to tell me quite seriously, “well Benny was a better clarinet player, but I was a better musician.” But at any rate you listened to a lot of that. You listened to a lot of Ellington. I mean I think the Ellington band was one of the first musics that I was conscious of. And then of course the other strange thing was I was going to clubs and hearing live music in New York on 52nd Street or at Nick’s in Greenwich Village at an obscenely early age because one of the things you’ve got to realize is that before World War II, before universal military service, nobody carried — and particularly in an area like New York where nobody had a driver’s license under any circumstances, nobody in Manhattan ever drove a car particularly in the 30s — there was nothing to card you with. We didn’t carry — nobody had the concept of carrying identification with you. So if you were — if you looked able to walk into the club and if you had the seventy-five cents that a drink would cost, nobody would give you a hard time. Or you learned. I mean some of those clip joints on 52nd Street no self-respecting child would want to be caught in. But Hickory House was a lovely, friendly place where the band played inside this big oval bar and if you got sort of off in the corner on a weekday night and you ordered a Tom Collins—
A tall one.

You learned the tallest drink to get. The bartender would leave you alone. So now that meant, Hickory House for example okay, Hickory House mid to late-30s, I’m listening to Joe Marsala, who not infrequently would have Bud Freeman, Dave Tough, and hey it was a long time before I realized that not every jazz band had a harpist in it. It was Joe’s wife.
Oh right.

Adele Girard played harp and was usually part of his band. But and then I discovered Nick’s and the whole point was also, see you could get in, a high school kid could get in there pretty easily, it was very inexpensive. It got to be, perhaps the music was secondary and in fact what a great place for a cheap date. So I do remember that that was part of the picture.
What’s a clip joint?
What’s a clip joint?
Yeah.
That’s — are you asking me seriously?
Yeah I am. I don’t know the term.

Well it’s a joint at which you get clipped. It’s a — you are aware of the reputation of the 52nd Street ex-speakeasy night clubs, and swing street and such, where oh just possibly the drinks were a little watered, just possibly you were being overcharged. That’s — I’m sorry I’m using old fashioned— © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-
No, I wanted to make sure what you were taking about.

Fine. Okay. The world has gone on to other forms of waylaying people. I mean I’m not old enough to have been around when the press gangs were kidnapping sailors and putting them on ships in the harbor, but this is almost it. But no the point is so what I’m saying is it’s a combination of a certain amount of osmosis. Pop music was in the air to a very large extent and it was very close to being or actually was jazz at this point, and then also physical circumstances made it possible for me to have direct listening experience even though it wasn’t an overwhelming love of music maybe that led me in there in the first place. But I heard it, I listened to it, so that by the time I got into the Army, which was when I was about like just short of being 21 when I got into the armed forces, I was sufficiently immersed in music at a time that, just a couple of years ago when a guy that I had been hanging out with a good deal in those days, in my Army days we lost sight of each other for decades and then re-encountered each other and we were reminiscing, actually strictly by mail, he lives in Europe now, but reminiscing about the old days and the thing that had been the first bond between us was the mutual love of the Ellington band. So that I was sufficiently into it. Then when I came out of the Army and went — my family was living in the immediate vicinity of Columbia University. I had graduated from Columbia. And I went back in the general campus area, after being in the armed forces I felt I had three years of total illiteracy. I had been an English major. I intended to go into some form of writing or publishing or whatnot, and I felt that I needed a kind of a crash course in being literate again. So I went back on campus, got into the graduate English school and wasn’t looking for a degree, didn’t stay there that long, but by doing that there was a group of people who I had known, not necessarily all that well but who I had known in the pre-war period which included Bill Grauer, who in the late 40s took over as publisher of a very esoteric jazz magazine called The Record Changer which basically it survived on the basis of having in its columns mail order buying, selling and auctioning of rare 78 old jazz records. And at that point I had gotten what I considered the proper kind of job for me, I was a young editor in a book publishing house. I like to say I worked at Simon & Schuster so long ago that I worked for Mr. Simon and Mr. Schuster and I really did. But I had this relationship going with — a working scene going with Grauer, for example, and I became editor of that publication. And among the things that happened early on was that Bill and I were invited down to the Greenwich Village home of Alfred and Lorraine Lion, because Alfred had just started to push Blue Note into modern jazz and we were claiming that The Record Changer would be open to considering all kinds of jazz, not just the traditional which it had previously been involved with. And so we were invited down there to meet and to listen to test pressings from the first recording session for Blue Note of Thelonious Monk. I was so damn dumb © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

in those days that I did not realize the impossibility of what I wisely set out to do, but on the spot it was a big, sprawling Greenwich Village studio living room, Monk and I went off into a corner disregarding all the other people there and I interviewed him for an article that appeared in the magazine. A number of years later when I had a fledgling record company and had heard the accurate rumor that Monk, who at that time was with Prestige, was very unhappy with where he was, they were not happy with him, he wasn’t selling records, at least he was a famous eccentric by that point, and they would be perfectly happy to get rid of him. But of course they wouldn’t have if they had known that another record company was interested. So we had a fairly clandestine meeting with Monk, sort of came to a gentleman’s agreement kind of situation, and what Prestige wanted was to be repaid not what — its royalty account was in the red, that’s always quite fictional — but the actual dollar amount that he had been over advanced by them which was $128 and change, so I gave him $130 and he went, actually the offices of Prestige were around the corner from the offices of Riverside in those days, he went around the corner and I still have in my possession — I insisted that he had to give me the original release letter, which had been prepared, saying your check for and then that was scratched out and cash was put in, a letter from Bob Weinstock to Thelonious Monk releasing him of his contractual obligations to Prestige. Monk then proceeded to sign with Riverside and in a very real sense that was the beginning of Riverside as a company to be taken seriously and it was, as far as I’m concerned, it was the beginning of my career as a jazz record producer. Now I had said previously to you that a lot of my life was accidental, that’s pretty damned accidental.
Well it’s almost like the fact that you were so new to it was to your advantage.

Well the interesting thing is that when we learned of the availability of, or potential availability of Monk, I had no idea that he would have any recollection of this whole initial encounter in light of that, but upon re-meeting him he proceeded to let us know he knew exactly who we were and he informed me that the article that I had written about him, not only obviously did he like it but he said it had been the first piece about him to ever appear in a national magazine. Well The Record Changer was a national magazine by courtesy. I suppose you could call it that, but the whole point was that it was the fact of my having done that bit of strange journalism that was the key thing. It meant that Monk remembered who I was, remembered me and the publication favorably and, you know, what the hell, was willing to take a chance with our scene.
And you made a transition yourself, like a lot of your colleagues, from being quote the moldy fig traditionalist listener, into a more modern style. Did it happen quickly for you?
Actually we can stay right with the same guy. As far as I’m concerned it primarily happened by way of Monk. Initially when I came back from the Pacific in 19— the © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

beginning of 1945 I guess or beginning of ’46, I’m sorry, the beginning of ’46, the people knowing that hey this is a guy that’s interested in jazz, you’ve got to hear what’s going on now. So I was forced to listen to a couple of the Dizzy Gillespie/Charlie Parker Guild records. And I thought this was some of the most outrageous noise I had ever heard. I had no ability to relate to it. And that didn’t mean anything to me and I continued in my set ways of believing that the world was bounded by nothing more extreme than Jelly Roll Morton, Louis Armstrong and Duke Ellington. That was about all I was willing to admit to. And by early in 1948 is when — the time of my meeting with Monk — it was the first time I’d heard Monk play. I listened to the test pressings of his first couple of Blue Note numbers and as it turns out I think one of the really important things that was involved there was that the drummer on that date was Art Blakey. So by God regardless of style, when Art Blakey played you were conscious of the beat and you were conscious of the rhythmic underpinning of that and somehow I was able to relate to what Monk was playing. Again I can’t particularly explain it to you, but this was the first modern jazz that I found attractive and interesting and I found myself able to digest. And it moved forward from that point. Now one of the strange things is I didn’t have too much of an awareness of Monk’s background and such. But a couple of years later the fourth album I did with Monk was a solo piano album. And in the course of one of those sessions he did an improvised blues. And standing in the control room to get a listening to a playback of that, Monk turned to me and said, “aah I sound just like James P. Johnson.” It was the first that I knew that Monk knew who the hell James P. Johnson was. But as it turned out Monk had grown up in the West Sixties in New York in the same area that Johnson lived in when Monk was a teenager. He could sneak in to this or that local bar and hear James P. He became quite fascinated and quite influenced by it, and there’s an awful lot of stride piano in Thelonious. But I was already pretty deeply involved with Monk before it was made clear to me how deliberate all this was. That he was in a sense a disciple or considered himself a disciple of James P. Johnson.
Well in your book you had said, “understanding the blues long has been the rule of thumb for evaluating jazz musicians.”
I still stick to that. There’s no reason to change that statement.
Right. So Thelonious certainly had a finger on the blues, at least what to do with it within his style.
Oh yeah. No question about that.
Let me go backwards just a little bit. You were in the South Pacific.
I was on Guam. I was a navigator radar operator on B-29s. I did a lot of dropping of bombs on Japan, which I’m resolutely not proud of for the rest of my life, so—
At that time you were 23? © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-
22 maybe, around in there.
How did you feel about it at the time?

At the time you didn’t feel about it. There is a — I mean I’m no great expert on it but there were two years in my life where I was involved in armed conflict and I think that one of the ways in which some of us emotionally survive was a form of anesthetizing yourself. You did not think about what you were doing. You did not — I mean I don’t think, unfortunately at the end of the war, after the war was over, I flew a couple of missions where we were taking a batch of generals up to evaluate what had been done to Tokyo. So we flew in the daytime at pretty low levels over Tokyo, which is something I had never done before, and I was able to see — see Tokyo, I’ll take a lot of credit for the fact that Tokyo was a modern city that is almost entirely a post-war city, it looked to me to be about fifty percent burned out, I mean put it that way. And that was the first time, the shock of that hit me. Not to turn this into too much of a war memoir but basically B- 29 flights were — we didn’t do very much daytime formation bombing which involved demolition bombs. We normally did night flights where you just flew in a single file so basically you were following at a decent interval the plane ahead of you and we were dropping incendiary bombs so that what you did was it was a very lazy form of bombing, you just dropped on the fires that were in front of you. And if the first guy in line had been way off target, we all were because nobody did anything else but that. But the whole point there was that you could be very detached. You didn’t have to force yourself to think that you really were causing fires to happen in a large metropolitan city that was there. And you could block that out pretty good because hey, you had no alternative. This is what you were doing and this is what you were doing in the great war and I’m not saying — I’ve long since given up figuring out whether this was in many respects a good or a bad thing. However, at this time of year as we get around the middle of August every year I am forced to think that in my personal opinion the damn atom bomb never should have been dropped, and let’s not get into the aesthetics or morality of that, but you have led me to this point in time so I make that statement. But you blot it out, the implications of what you were doing, I think because it was pretty necessary.
Right. Were the Japanese putting up a defense against your planes at that time?

In the latter stages no. There was always a fair amount of antiaircraft fire but not — there were virtually no fighter planes. I mean the Japanese Air Force was pretty much shot to hell in the last months of the war which is when I was primarily — the time I was primarily there. But let’s get back to jazz.

All right. The early things with Monk certainly must have opened your ears up and it seems like some of the stuff that he taught you might not have been apparent right at that © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-
time? Was there kind of like a delay in certain incidents where you understood afterwards what he was trying to show you?

Well no, when I talk about learning from Monk, to me the most important learning from Monk that I did was a matter of learning attitudes. Learning how to conduct myself in the studio in relation to the important, demanding, impatient artist, which is what all good artists should be. And it wasn’t so much — I did discover for example that — eventually I discovered that the main cause of Monk’s impatience, and his impatience with his fellow musicians, was that as far as he was concerned there wasn’t anything that difficult about his music. He grasped it. How come you couldn’t? One of my favorite lines which happens to have survived on a scrap of tape from a session that Coleman Hawkins and John Coltrane were involved in is Hawkins had been having trouble with the turnaround on one particular number and Monk can be heard saying to him, “whatsa matter? You’re supposed to be the great Coleman Hawkins. How come you can’t play that?” He didn’t say you’re the great Coleman Hawkins how come you can’t — you’re supposed to be the great Coleman Hawkins. I’ve always treasured that remark. But fundamentally it’s that I, again, understanding what I consider to be the root causes of his impatience which were that he didn’t know what the hell was it that was giving you this trouble. I’m not having any trouble with this. And that he was an excellent teacher as far as logistics is concerned. I learned how to conduct myself in the studio, I learned when to push, when not to push, and how much of that has got to be instinctive and is a matter of reading what the artist has in mind, and I also learned to be very wary of arbitrary musical judgements. I think this is perhaps one of the things that has led to my lifelong distaste for and distrust of jazz criticism. Because it has always been full of people who feel that it’s necessary for them to strike a pose, to take a position, to give us THE judgment from heaven as to whether this is good or that is bad or whatnot. And you know that’s not necessary. And it’s never been necessary. Music is something that gets evaluated very personally. I mean yeah, proficient playing and non-proficient playing is generally, you can make distinctions there, except a hell of a lot of people spent a lot of time in the early days saying that Monk couldn’t play the piano and they were wrong. But in general I just feel that — now value judgements are very important. I have lots of value judgements and have always made such judgements, and I have only under very rare and unusual circumstances allowed myself to get involved professionally with a musician that I didn’t have strong positive feelings for, but that didn’t necessarily have to involve compatibility between two — I can approve of two musicians who wouldn’t necessarily approve of each other, approaching them from — and I’ve never felt it necessary for there to be an arbitrary set of standards and I’m very wary of judging performances. I will judge an artist. I fundamentally, if I, in my years as somebody who was involved with scouting © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

and signing artists, I approved of somebody, I liked what he was doing, I felt it made sense to me, should make sense to the world, I was willing to get involvement there, then I’m making a commitment at that point. That commitment involves working with that artist, getting from him as well as giving to him, but it does not necessarily involve my deciding that what he is doing at a given moment is good or bad, whether it meets with my approval is pretty God damned irrelevant. I am not more gifted than the artist in determining — this is a hard thing to articulate — I’m not talking about suspension of judgement. What I’m saying is I tend to make my judgements initially. I may revise them later but let’s let that go for the moment. If I have felt strongly enough positively about an artist to want to become involved in working with him that involves approving his taste. It has to involve approving his judgement. Therefore it involves that I am not going to nickel and dime the situation and decide that on this particular point I really know better than he does. And that’s where I part company with the people who feel that the only way they’re going to make their living is by making immediate sweeping judgements.
Isn’t part of your role in that situation to know not necessarily what is best, it’s what that performer is best — what his best is?

Yeah. Well again, when I speak of myself as a catalytic agent it’s endeavoring to provide the circumstances under which the artist can deliver to the best of his ability, not distracted or sidetracked or disturbed. And that implies of course — not necessarily my approval of what he is doing, it implies my approval of the rightness of his doing what he chooses to do.
Well Thelonious was apparently, in a lot of cases, hard to play with? Hard to get used to? Is that a fair statement?

No. Because first of all there was — working with Thelonious was not something that you did, I mean you being another musician, very arbitrarily or casually. If you were playing in a band with Monk or on a record date with Monk it was based on his awareness of you and his approval and his considering that it was likely that you would be able to perform his music. Because again, playing with Monk involved one of two things. Either playing Monk compositions or playing standards that he found he could adapt. So that the hard part sort of came first. It came before you got to the starting gate. I don’t think it’s fair to say that people found it hard playing with him. First of all people that were invited to play with him generally turned out to have the ability to do so. But in a sense we had been working together back in the old days too. So I would say that what happened to his career, it’s always been tragic the way it was cut short. The man had a stroke and never regained consciousness. And he was only in his 40s. But I didn’t feel badly about that, I felt I wasn’t happy with what happened to Monk’s career at Columbia where for the most part, there were a few exceptions and there were a couple of interesting big band things, but for the most part it was the working group over and over again, and Monk and I had been very happy with the variations that we were able to do and the interesting guests and associations that we were able to bring in, I just think that what happened there was he took the path of least resistance, nobody really gave him — because there were some large things where like “Big Band at Lincoln Center,” a live performance big band stuff. The final Monk record for Columbia which was the Oliver Nelson arrangements I thought just lost the whole spirit of Monk so badly that it was not a good record. But I guess there was a case where the artist left his association with me primarily because the people who were running his career then feeling it was time to take © Fillius Jazz Archive -23-

him up a notch to a major label, and he was pulled away from us. And I didn’t think anything sensible or helpful or intelligent was done to his career subsequently. Bill Evans also went on to a — although there what happened was he kind of knew that he was kind of good in the sense that even though when Bill first went to Verve, and that was a matter of Bill left Riverside with a year to go on his contract which was because we were in existence, we were starting to have real money problems and frankly Bill had turned into one of the most expensive junkies I ever had to be involved with, represented more of a burden than we really could comfortably handle. I mean I have said this and I’ve written about this before, it’s not anything new, but being his record company, his friend, and his producer all at the same time was a hell of a strain on me. And what happened was with a year to go and Creed Taylor was extremely anxious to have Bill as his artist, and bring him over to Verve, so that a buyout kind of thing was arranged. It’s interesting and shows the passage of time. In a sense this is related to what had happened eight years earlier with Riverside buying Monk out of his Prestige contract but the amounts were hugely different. But Bill, what happened there as far as the artistic content, after a very little while something, and I never have felt it was any of my business even knowing, but something was not right in the working relationship between Bill and his producer there, and Bill’s manager, a woman who was very, very important in his life, Helen Keane, took over as Bill’s producer and actually did serve as a producer of the rest of his output. That included a funny period, he also was at Fantasy in the early 70s, and actually I think Helen and I intended to co-produce a live date together. Bill was recorded — well we initially intended to record it at Shelly’s Manne-Hole in Los Angeles but Shelly’s had just moved from its original funky location into the basement of a bank building and there was a big — the air conditioning equipment broke down and the whole floor of the club was covered in about a foot of oil out of the equipment. So we canceled that one out and ended up recording him at the Vanguard and Helen got sick and didn’t make it so I ended up doing that one by myself. So we never did get to co-produce it, which probably was a good idea. But Bill actually was pretty — see Bill knew what he wanted and was pretty insistent on it as Cannon was. Well “Peace Piece” is literally what it always was identified as being. “Peace Piece” was an improvisation, it is true that what he was setting out to do was to create an introduction to a recording of “Some Other Time,” the Leonard Bernstein, Comden and Green song. He started messing around and found that gee, this was something very interesting in and of itself so that literally that was created at the record date. I mean nobody went in there with the intention — now actually the title was in existence but not to be used on that tune. There is a solo piece called “Epilogue” which is on the end of each side of that album originally. That was originally going to be called “Peace Piece.” So the title was there and then this thing was created, and this goes much better with that title, but it literally was a spontaneously generated thing. And the interesting part of that is, a couple of interesting stories. One is although unfortunately the tape for some reason did not survive as sometimes happens, nobody thought in terms of alternates and whatnot, “Peace Piece” as issued is approximately fifty percent from one take and fifty percent from another. If you like the beginning of — I think he just did it twice. He liked the beginning of one, liked the end of the other, obviously no problem splicing together. But it sure would have been nice at some stage of the game to be able to issue the rejected halves, but they did not survive for whatever reason. And that frequently happens. Oh yeah, session takes that the good things have been taken out of, where are they? It doesn’t matter. So that is one point. Also he maintained for years that he couldn’t play it again because it had never been notated and it just existed as free improvisation. Towards the end though I do believe he had gotten himself to where he played it, he re-created it and played it a few times. But essentially it was what it was, a total improvisation starting from an initial concept which was that he was trying to do something that would fit as an intro to “Some Other Time.”

What was the typical budget? I don’t know if you can say typical?

You can’t do that for several reasons. One reason you can’t do that is that I’m talking now basically late 50s, early 60s, the value of the dollar is so outrageously different that you can’t make comparisons. Even if you allow for this, that or the other, you lose all sense of — I mean there were no journeymen ball players making over a million dollars a year in those days, just to take an example of the world of entertainment and how things have changed. Also another thing I like to point out was that now there’s a lot, because like I say everything was a lot cheaper but it didn’t really mean that much because the standard of living was different, everything cost less, but what it really boils down to is you got paid less for things. It was fourteen cents for a loaf of bread or whatever, but the fact of the matter is when you get down to the irreducible minimum and it’s still dollars that are being paid, the difference is important, so that it is relevant to point out that union scale for a musician recording, a sideman doing three hours of work in which fifteen minutes of music for an album could be created, scale was $41.25. Now that was not outrageously bad but it just — what is scale today?
I don’t know anymore. It’s a lot more than that.

Well the scale today is several hundred dollars. So that whatever, and I must confess I should know better but I’ve gotten to the point where the reason I’m not — I mean I still do a certain amount of recording but I’ve gotten into the habit where you pay sidemen a lump sum that is never going to be as small as what scale is so I mean I don’t even deal in terms of thinking about things that way. Nevertheless the whole point is that we did records very economically. Let’s put it that way. The fact is that you could do a trio record and your musicians costs might total $500. You know you might roughly speaking be paying $125 to each sideman and $250 to the leader and that’s probably what got paid on the first Bill Evans album. And nothing — nobody was exploiting anybody. It also meant that even though the record only sold 800 copies in the first year, so we didn’t come out ahead on it, but it was not unthinkable to say let’s continue working with this guy. Because he deserves to be recorded. So you can’t — and I do absolutely refuse to try and translate — it would take, maybe if I got on somebody’s program sometime in the presence of let’s say a jazz fan who was also a significant economist, we could have a discussion about that, and I’d love to do that sometime. Unfortunately I’ve never ever come across such a person. I would love to talk with such a person and it certainly should be, by all means, should be a public conversation — a lot of people — I would love to know more myself about what that relationship is. What I do know is this, I know it was possible to make jazz records without having any significant or even noticeable amount of capitalization. That’s the important fact. That a bunch of young guys with a lot of balls and ambition and love of the music and very little capital were able to create record © Fillius Jazz Archive -26-

companies. That could not happen today even though people are constantly still trying to do it. And there were a number of other factors you see. We were kind of famous for not having rehearsals. Even though there was written material but what you have to point out then is we were working and made sure we were working with people who were tremendously familiar with playing with each other. If I had a rhythm section that technically didn’t have a rehearsal they nevertheless had been playing together probably for about ten years, that’ll do as far as being able to get things out of each other and being able to work together. And that would be not that easy to do today, though there is still a tendency, I mean I fight hard to get — to work with people who know each other who can shortcut the time and don’t have to be introduced to each other at the date, but you just won’t get back to — that was the climate. I mean the scene in New York was a very real part of what we did, a lot of interaction between a lot of talented musicians. And again at Riverside there was a tremendous amount of people associated with the label playing on other people’s dates, not because we asked them to because they told us — I’m going to be — I mean the second record I did with Jimmy Heath, who everybody really loved, was because Jimmy was such a great writer we just pulled it together and got Jimmy, we did like a ten-piece date, seven horns kind of thing. And it was easy, we knew who the bass player and the drummer were going to be, they were going to be Percy and Tootie [Heath], but there were two trumpets on that album called “Really Big,” which is a wonderful, medium band, Jimmy Heath album from about 1961. Well the trumpet players on that are Nat Adderley and Clark Terry because they told me they were going to be. The alto is Cannonball because he said so. And Cannonball only plays one solo on the thing. We were not trying to milk the famous artist and have this really, like it was featuring him or something. But there he was because he damn well said he was going to be there. And I think for some reason we changed piano players between sessions so we had I think Flanagan on one and Cedar Walton on the other, that kind of thing. Now some of that is like names didn’t have the same meaning that they do today. I mean everybody says wow, a Thelonious Monk record with John Coltrane and Coleman Hawkins on it. Wow. Well it’s a wonderful record but it was not a record that was made with two famous tenor players. It was a record made with one tenor player who was considered to be over the hill, and one who hadn’t happened yet. But those are important points to remember when you’re milking the nostalgia of an old cat like me to remember that a lot of times you have to look below the surface. It’s the same as don’t take Miles Davis’ word for anything. Investigate what the truth of it is. It’s the same kind of situation. Don’t just look at the personnel listing and say wow, those guys must have spent a lot of money to put this band together.

Well this has been a great pleasure. I could easily continue endlessly but I don’t know if you necessarily want me to. But I have enjoyed it. I hope all kinds of good things are made of things. And I do want to end up with a copy of what I have said.
Absolutely. You know jazz has been elevated, or whatever, I’m not sure of the right word, to a high state of art these days. Do you think it’s been positive for jazz?

That’s a hard question to answer. I do feel that when I have attended the last few jazz educators conventions and I am pleased to see — I used to frown on jazz education because those God damn stage band so-called which were nothing but tired old big band charts and there were important things like the fact that if it wasn’t for North Texas State how would Woody Herman ever get new players for his band, all those cliches of the past. But the fact is I think that to some degree jazz education has done a wonderful job, it has progressed, there are people learning things on stages of the game where people never were learning before. As long as you recognize there is only one of a series of tools and it is by no means like is that the only way to go, so that I would say on the whole, hey, if you asked me did I think that multi-track recordings was a positive or a negative experience I’d say pretty much the same thing. If you keep it under control it’s just fine. If you use it, if you don’t let it use you, if you use the fact of jazz education, the proliferation of it in so many places, if you use that to the purposes of making good jazz it’s fine. But don’t let it run away with you. I guess that’s — I feel that way about technical progress, I mean I love digital recording, I have always been of several minds about multi-track for just that reason, I don’t want the bass player to be able to punch in the right notes, I want it to be important what notes he was playing when they were listening to him while they were playing. So that makes me an anachronism in some ways I know. But so be it.
